steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The new lighthouse had no ghosts, or so they’d told Elias when he signed the papers.

“Steel and glass,” the harbormaster had said, clapping him on the shoulder. “Solid-state beacons. LED arrays. No room for spirits in that sort of thing.”

Elias had only nodded. He wasn’t worried about spirits. He was worried about silence.

The sea tower stood half a mile off the coast, bolted into a black tooth of rock the locals called Widow’s Fang. It rose clean and white from the Atlantic, a straight, modern cylinder unlike the crumbling stone beacons Elias had known as a young man. Those had smelled of whale oil and damp clothing, of rust and old books. This smelled of paint, plastic, and disinfectant.

Still, the waves below were the same, rolling up and smashing themselves to gray foam against the rock as they’d done long before any light had been raised.

“They’ll automate it fully next year,” the harbormaster had said casually. “Until then, it’s a good posting. Quiet. You’ll like it.”

Elias had not corrected him. Liking and needing were different things.

He arrived in late autumn, when the sky was the color of wet paper and the wind had teeth. The supply boat left him with a duffel, three crates of provisions, a toolbox, and a laminated emergency procedure sheet that fluttered angrily in the wind as if offended by its own bureaucracy.

When the engine of the boat faded into the distance, the silence rushed in like a tide. It filled the space between his heartbeat and his thoughts. The lighthouse rose above him, humming faintly with the low, constant power of its rotating lamp.

He climbed the interior spiral stairs slowly, each step hollow and ringing. The walls were smooth, white metal. No carved initials. No dates. No stories. At the top, the lantern room was a bright, sterile hemisphere of glass. The beacon assembly was housed in a metal frame, lenses and panels glinting.

He checked the control panel—green lights, all of them—and stood looking out at the horizon. A strip of dull silver where sea and sky met. He took a deep breath.

“Hello, then,” he said softly, as if addressing the horizon itself. “It’s you and me.”

The routine settled around him within days. At dawn, he checked the panels and power backups. At noon, he logged visibility, wind speed, passing vessels. At dusk, he delivered his brief voice report over the radio: “Widow’s Fang Light, operational. Visibility eight miles. No anomalies.”

No one ever replied. The radio crackled, hissed, and fell quiet.

He cooked simple meals on the tiny steel stove. He made coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in. He read the same three books in rotation. At night, after his checks, he climbed back to the lantern room and sat in the metal chair bolted to the floor, watching the beam sweep its slow, steady arc across the water.

On clear nights, he could see its flash reflected in the windows of the town along the shore, little points of yellow and orange. He imagined the people there, closing curtains, washing dishes, arguing in kitchens, watching televisions, tucking children into bed. The light passed over them, indifferent but faithful.

Every twelve seconds, the beam swept, as the manual described: a constant pattern, seven-tenths of a second on, eleven-point-three seconds off. The rhythm embedded itself into Elias’s pulse. He timed his breathing to it. Inhale—flash—exhale.

One night in early December, as a storm grumbled on the horizon, the light stuttered.

Elias was halfway through a chapter, propped in his bunk, when he felt it rather than saw it—a hesitation in the machinery above, a tiny change in the sound. The hum climbed half a note and dropped, like a throat clearing.

He froze. Closed the book without marking his place. Climbed.

The lantern room was an echoing globe of shadow and glass. The panels clicked and turned in their track. The lamp burned steady. The green lights on the panel still shone.

He squinted at the sea. Far out, where the sky sagged low and dark, a wall of rain moved toward him. He glanced down at the control board. Everything read nominal.

Then the beacon flickered.

It was just a blink, as if the light had shut its eyes for the space of one second too long between sweeps. Not a full outage. Just…a skipped breath.

Elias checked the wiring. He opened the access panel and listened to the electric whine. He ran diagnostics on the control unit he barely understood. “Fault tolerance,” the harbormaster had said. “You’re mostly a caretaker. The systems take care of themselves.”

But an automated system did not feel what Elias felt then: a prickle along the scalp, a sense of something unsettled in the air.

He reported the flicker in his nightly call. There was no answer.

The storm hit after midnight.

Rain lashed the glass, a frantic drumming that turned the world outside opaque. The wind howled around the tower, grabbed the structure in both hands and shook it. The sea hurled itself at the rock below, blind and furious.

Inside, the light kept turning. Elias watched each rotation with the intensity of a surgeon monitoring a failing heart. Flash, dark, flash—no more flicker. He sagged in his chair.

At three in the morning, lightning hit the sea so close he saw it even with his eyes shut. The tower trembled. The overhead lights cut out, plunging the stairwell into sudden, absolute dark.

The beacon died.

The absence slammed into him physically. The hum ceased. The faint warmth the lamp gave off disappeared. The roar of the storm, freed from the subtle anchor of the machine noise, doubled.

For several heartbeats Elias sat motionless, his mind empty of everything but a single, animal panic: the ships.

He lurched to the control panel. Dead. The small green eyes of the system were gone, replaced by a flat, unhelpful blackness. Emergency power should have kicked in automatically, but there was nothing.

He grabbed his flashlight from the wall hook, thumbed it on, and scraped the beam over the breakers. The instructions were printed in plasticked letters beside them: in case of main failure, engage auxiliary generator. He flipped the switch. Listened.

The generator coughed below, somewhere in the belly of the tower. Sputtered. Fell silent.

Another switch. Another cough, weaker. The storm laughed around him.

He stared out at the wildly churning darkness where the beam should have been dancing. The sea, deprived of that single, revolving reassurance, looked like an endless, hungry thing.

“Come on,” he said aloud—to the generator, to the tower, to himself. “Come on, now.”

He ran.

Down the stairwell, the flashlight made a narrow tunnel of light. Every footstep echoed. The air smelled of salt and oil and the sharp ozone trace of the lightning strike.

The generator room was a cramped steel box near the base of the tower, half a floor above the rock itself. The generator sat hulking and sullen in the corner, red indicator light dark. Elias dragged the maintenance manual off its hook, flipped to the emergency start procedure with hands that wanted to shake, forced them not to.

Air in. Fuel check. Manual crank.

He yanked the starter handle, muscles burning. The machine wheezed, clanked, refused.

Above, without the beacon’s constant sweep, the storm felt closer. As if the dark had shifted in toward Widow’s Fang, sniffing at it.

He tried again, and again, until his breath came heavy. The generator hacked feebly to life for three seconds, then shuddered still.

Something else moved under the storm’s voice. A distant, low horn.

He froze. Strained to hear it again.

There. Somewhere out in the darkness, a ship was sounding its presence, low and insistent.

The chart on the wall upstairs flashed into his memory, the shipping lane that passed within a few miles of Widow’s Fang. In this visibility, with radar cluttered and the seas heaving, a captain might make the light his primary reference. A fixed star on a storm-torn map.

And there was no light.

He dropped the useless handle. Raced back up the stairs, two at a time, flashlight beam jerking. His lungs burned, but the thought of that horn, calling blind in the dark, burned hotter.

At the small storeroom halfway up, he skidded to a halt. His shoulder slammed the doorframe.

An older protocol, from an older posting, rose in his mind like a voice: if the main beacon fails and auxiliary cannot be engaged, the keeper will provide a temporary visual signal by any available means.

Any available means.

He flung the storage door open. The beam swung crazily over shelves of spare bulbs, cleaning supplies, coils of rope. At the back, under a tarp, a box of things from the previous lighthouse, relics the modernization crew hadn’t bothered to remove.

His light paused on metal. Reflective glass. Old lenses.

And there, lying on its side, was a brass-handled handlamp. The sort his father had once carried up damp stone steps, night after night.

He pulled it free. It was heavy and cold. Inside, the bulb was intact. The power cord ended in a frayed, outdated plug that had nowhere to go in the new tower’s plastic sockets.

Elias ran his fingers along its weight, thinking. Then his hand found the spare battery pack for the external floodlights, square and solid in its charging cradle.

He exhaled through his teeth. “We’re going to make this work,” he murmured, to the lamp, to the tower, to whatever might be listening.

He stripped the cord with his pocketknife, fingers clumsy but persistent. Hooked bare wires to battery terminals. Tiny sparks snapped, bit his knuckles. The storm roared approval.

For a heartbeat, nothing. Then the lamp’s bulb glowed dully, as if waking from a long sleep. He angled it, and the glow strengthened, a focused beam punching a small, defiantly bright hole into the darkness of the storeroom.

It was pitiful compared to the dead giant above, a candle beside a searchlight. It was also what he had.

He took the lamp in one hand, the battery pack in the other, and climbed.

The lantern room was a glass globe hammered by rain. Without the main light, it felt huge and cold. The sea smashed white around the black rock below. The sky was a single moving bruise.

Elias set the battery down, wiped water from his face, and thought about pattern.

Seven-tenths on. Eleven-point-three off.

All up and down this coast, captains and mates had memorized the language of those patterns. Each light was a signature. Widow’s Fang Light: one short flash every twelve seconds. In good weather, a sailor could match that to the chart. In bad weather, one familiar wink in the chaos could feel like a handshake from shore.

He could not rebuild the beacon. He could not fix the generator in this storm. But he could, perhaps, keep its promise.

He checked his watch. The luminous hands crept past three-twenty. He did the math in his head—seven-tenths of a second, three-quarters almost. A count, then: one—on—two through twelve—off.

The horn sounded again, closer.

Elias stepped to the glass, raised the lamp, took a breath.

“One,” he whispered, and threw the beam across the water. Held it. “Two,” he began the silent count, and snapped it off before he reached two. He watched the dark, hand shaking slightly, not from fear but from the cold.

He counted to twelve. He lifted the lamp again.

“One.”

On. Off.

Twelve.

On. Off.

Outside, the storm raged, indifferent. But his small, precise defiance continued. The beam carved fragile spokes through the rain, marking Widow’s Fang like a heartbeat on the black sea.

He lost feeling in his fingers first. Then in his toes. The wind drove the rain horizontally; even inside the glass, a fine mist gathered. His hair clung to his forehead. Water tickled a path down his back.

He did not stop.

Somewhere in the stretch between the fifty-third and fifty-fourth flash, doubt snuck in. Perhaps the ship’s radar was fine. Perhaps they’d altered course hours ago, giving Widow’s Fang a wide berth. Perhaps no one was there to see this feeble imitation of a proper light.

His arm burned. His elbow ached. The horn sounded again, much nearer now, and something in its voice—urgent, uncertain—drove the doubt away.

On. Off.

On. Off.

Minutes crawled past, or hours, or both. The pattern held. His counts became a metronome in his skull. His world narrowed until there was nothing but the lamp in his hand, the black arch of time between each flash, the whistle of wind, the faint taste of metal at the back of his throat.

Then, suddenly, a ghost responded.

Far out in the boiling dark, at the ragged edge of his lamp’s reach, a white flare rose, hung, and fell. A rocket. Another followed, red, then white again, painting the undersides of the clouds for a breath-long moment.

Elias’s fingers tightened on the handle. A distress signal. Not just a ship passing by: a ship in trouble.

He forced his voice steady and went to the radio. The power light stubbornly glowed on its separate reserve; at least that system had held.

“Any vessel in vicinity of Widow’s Fang Light,” he said, breathless, leaning close to the microphone. “Your flares are observed. Lighthouse power failure in progress. Manual light is operating at reduced range. State your position.”

Static rushed back. Then, crackling through, a strained voice:

“This is the trawler Maribel. Taking on water. Engines disabled. We’ve lost radar in the interference. We…we can see some kind of light. We’re not sure if we’re moving toward it or—”

A roar of background noise swallowed the rest.

Elias cut in. “Maintain your current heading relative to that light,” he said, gripping the mic. “That’s Widow’s Fang. You’re south of it. The rock is north-northeast. Do you have any engine control at all?”

“Port engine intermittently,” came the ragged reply. “Steering sluggish.”

“Then listen,” Elias said. “Do exactly as I say. When my light flashes three times quickly, you will turn ten degrees to port. When it flashes twice, ten degrees to starboard. One long flash, hold course. Understood?”

A pause. “Understood.”

He laid the microphone down, his hand leaving a damp print on the plastic. Went back to the glass, to his makeshift star. The storm crashed and screamed, but a new thread had woven into its noise: a human voice, shaky yet alive, anchored to his.

He adjusted his counts. One—manual beacon: on—off. Pause. Pause. Then three quick flashes, wrist snapping, muscles protesting. Three quick instructions: port. Port. Port.

He timed them carefully, listening between for the answering horn blast: one long, one long, two short. Any sign the trawler had heard, had obeyed.

The pattern became a conversation. Single pulse: hold. Triple: veer left. Double: veer right. In the darkness beyond his glass world, somewhere beneath the boiling clouds and hammering rain, a small, wounded boat altered its path again and again, pulled not by stars but by a tired man with a borrowed lamp.

Once he miscounted. Only realized when his own internal rhythm tripped over itself. He cursed softly, corrected, sent another set of signals, hoping the captain on the Maribel had more sense and less desperation than to follow a single anomalous flash.

“Widow’s Fang, we see rocks—” the radio yelped at one point, voice rising sharp with fear.

“Then you’re too far north,” Elias snapped. “Hold course on my next long beam, then respond when you’ve got clear water under you.”

They danced like that for a while—how long, he couldn’t later say. Time frayed in the storm’s hands. His whole body shook, whether from cold or exhaustion or the enormous, stupid intensity of trying to be a lighthouse on his own, he could not have said.

Then, through an odd interlude of lighter rain, he saw them.

Just visible when his handlamp flared: the vague bulk of a vessel, riding low and awkward in the waves, maybe a quarter mile out. The portholes showed no light. The mastrits jerked like broken fingers against the sky.

He held his arm as high as it would go and gave one long, steady beam, knuckles white on the handle. The trawler’s stern swung, the line of its bow shifting, aligning away from the darker patch of water that hid Widow’s Fang’s submerged teeth.

Another wave rose and crashed, briefly obscuring it. When it fell, the boat had passed the worst of the rocky outcrops.

“Maribel, what’s your status?” he called, lips numb.

On the radio, a voice broke and laughed in the same breath. “We’re clear of the rocks. Still taking water, but we’ve got a heading. Coast Guard cutter says they’ve got our signal and are inbound. We…we saw you. Whatever you’re doing up there, keep doing it.”

Elias let out a breath that felt like it had been lodged under his ribs all his life. “I will,” he said simply.

He kept the improvised pattern going until the faint outline of a cutter materialized, hull cutting through the seas with purpose. Its own bright lights dwarfed his; the white beam from its searchlight swept past Widow’s Fang, firm and blinding, making his little handlamp seem like a child’s toy in comparison.

Only then did he allow his arm to drop.

He stayed until he saw the Maribel’s silhouette draw up alongside the cutter, until he watched, in disjointed flashes, the shapes of people become smaller shapes crossing the gap, a line here, a stagger there. Until the combined mass of the two boats turned, angled back toward the distant smear of shoreline lights.

The storm began, reluctantly, to unravel. The wind, as if exhausted by its own fury, dropped a note. The rain eased from needles into fat, plopping drops. Out between sky and sea, a suggestion of gray crept back, replacing black.

Elias sank into the metal chair, the handlamp resting in his lap, its bulb finally flickering, dimming. His shoulder throbbed. His knees ached. He felt, in that quiet after-clamor, like the lighthouse itself: upright, hollow, ringing softly with the aftermath of violence.

He must have dozed, because he woke to a different hum. A low, steady vibration underfoot. The faint click and whir of relays resetting.

The main beacon blinked on.

It happened gradually, as systems rebooted. First a hesitation, then a low growl from below as the generator finally caught and held, the room lights flick
